summary_html: Cases arising on **federal lands/facilities** or involving **Indian children** invoke federal/tribal jurisdictional rules (VICAA for federal facilities; **ICWA** for Indian children and tribal preference/jurisdiction).
authority_html:
- **VICAA (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — federal-facility reporting mandates  
- **ICWA (25 U.S.C. §§ 1901–1963)** — tribal jurisdiction, placement preferences, notice to tribes

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Domicile under ICWA is a matter of uniform federal law; because the twins took their mother's reservation domicile at birth the tribal court had exclusive jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a) and the state adoption decree had to be vacated.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling authority on when an Indian child's case must go to tribal rather than District court at the threshold.
key_cases.quote: the twin babies in this case were domiciled on the reservation when adoption proceedings were begun, the Choctaw tribal court possessed exclusive jurisdiction

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court rejected every challenge to the Indian Child Welfare Act, upholding Congress's Article I power and rejecting the anticommandeering claims on the merits while dismissing the equal protection and nondelegation claims for lack of standing.
key_cases.relevance: It confirms that ICWA's active-efforts, expert-witness and placement-preference commands remain binding on courts handling Indian child custody proceedings.
key_cases.quote: we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that ICWA § 1912(f)'s continued-custody standard does not apply where the Indian parent never had custody of the child and that § 1912(d)'s active-efforts requirement applies only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an existing Indian family, so neither provision barred termination of the biological father's rights.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Supreme Court's construction of ICWA's active-efforts and continued-custody commands, which Holyfield (jurisdiction) and Brackeen (constitutionality) leave undefined, and it tells a District practitioner when those heightened duties actually attach.
key_cases.quote: Consistent with the statutory text, we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family's "breakup" would be precipitated by the termination of the parent's rights.

mandatory_reporters: Employee, agent, or contractor of the Child and Family Services Agency — D.C. Code § 4-1321.02(a)
Individual involved in the care and treatment of patients
Humane officer of any agency charged with the enforcement of animal cruelty laws
Employee of the Department of Parks and Recreation
Any person 18 or older, for suspected sexual abuse of a child under 16 — D.C. Code § 22-3020.52(a)
reporting_details: The District is not a universal-reporter jurisdiction: D.C. Code § 4-1321.02(a) names 19 categories of mandatory reporter, who report abuse, neglect, sexual abuse, or a non-accidental bullet, knife, or sharp-object injury to CFSA or the Metropolitan Police Department under § 4-1321.02(b)(1)(A), (C), and (D), but must report to CFSA alone when a child aged 5 through 13 has 10 or more days of unexcused absences within a school year — § 4-1321.02(b)(1)(B), the District's truancy trigger. D.C. Code § 22-3020.52(a) separately requires any person 18 or older to report suspected sexual abuse of a child under 16 (both terms defined in § 22-3020.51), a call to 911 or a report to CFSA counting as a report to the police.
